extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of scientific method; philosophers of science; experimental scientists
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and practical guidance for discovering laws of causation by observation and experiment, including how causes combine, when compositional reasoning applies, and how to train/perform observation and experimental separation. Focuses on the analytic steps required for induction and the limits of deductive prediction in different domains (mechanics, chemistry, physiology, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition of Causes
rubrics_metrics.description: When several causes operate jointly, the joint effect is identical with the sum of their separate effects provided the same law that expresses each cause's separate effect also expresses its part in the joint effect; exemplified in mechanical phenomena (communication of motion/forces).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use compositional reasoning (deduction) in domains where separate-cause laws continue to hold in combination — e.g., dynamics: forces add vectorially; weight is additive. If you know the effect of each cause alone, you can often predict their combined effect by 'casting up the results.' Examples: two perpendicular forces produce combined displacement equal to vector sum; the weight of a compound equals sum of element weights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heteropathic (Non-compositional) Combinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Cases in which the conjoint action of causes produces effects heterogeneous to, or different from, the sum of their separate effects; the combination may give rise to entirely new laws (e.g., chemical compounds, living organisms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not attempt simple summation of separate-agent laws in these cases. Expect novel properties (qualitative changes) when ingredients are combined in certain ways — e.g., hydrogen + oxygen → water with properties unlike either element; mixing two liquids producing a solid. Such cases require direct experiment rather than pure deduction from component laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two Modes of Conjunct Action / Mutual Interference
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two distinct ways concurrent causes can interact: (1) additive/compositional, where each cause exerts full efficacy and joint effect is sum (including differences via algebraic subtraction), and (2) heteropathic, where conjoining causes abolishes previous laws and produces new phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When causes act in opposition, treat one effect as negative and compose algebraically (e.g., inlet vs drain in a reservoir). Recognize which mode applies before inferring joint outcomes; misuse leads to incorrect inferences about causation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of Proportionality of Effects to Causes
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine that effects are proportional to causes is a particular case of the Composition of Causes and holds only where causes are homogeneous and composition applies; it fails when increasing a cause changes the kind of effect (thresholds producing qualitatively different outcomes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid assuming linear proportionality across regimes where additional quantity alters effect type (e.g., small heat increases expansion, larger heat melts, still larger heat decomposes). Use compositional assumption only within the domain where the same laws apply continuously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deductive vs Empirical Character of Sciences Depends on Compositionality
rubrics_metrics.description: Mechanics is largely deductive because composition of causes holds; chemistry and physiology are less deductive (historically) because conjunctions often produce new laws, though derived laws may themselves become composable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a field's phenomena largely obey composition-of-causes, pursue deductive/theoretical derivations. In domains where heteropathic laws dominate, prioritize experimental discovery of intermediate/general laws (e.g., law of definite proportions) that can raise the field toward deductive status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possibility of Higher-level Laws Becoming Composable
rubrics_metrics.description: Heteropathic laws (those arising from combinations) may themselves be subject to composition with one another, so fields like chemistry or physiology might eventually become partly deductive once appropriate intermediate laws are discovered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Search for generalizations (e.g., Dalton's law of definite proportions, isomorphism, Berthollet's law) that relate compound properties to elements; these can serve as premises enabling wider deductive reasoning in formerly empirical domains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction as the Determination of Laws of Causation
rubrics_metrics.description: The main business of induction is to ascertain which causes are correctly assigned to which effects — that is, to determine the laws of causation (effects of causes, and causes of effects).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame induction as resolving complex antecedent–consequent uniformities into simpler causal relations. The objective is to acquire premises (laws of causation) from which many uniformities and predictions can be deduced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observation Requires Mental Analysis (Decomposition) First
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective observation begins with an intellectual partition: resolving complex phenomena into component facts, antecedents, and consequents before attempting to find invariant connections among them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always perform a careful mental analysis before experimenting. Identify distinct antecedents and consequents; avoid taking the chaotic whole as unanalyzed. This mental partition is indispensable though not sufficient for discovering causal relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experiment is Separation in Nature to Test Causal Relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Beyond mental partition, one must separate facts from one another 'in nature' — i.e., by experiment — to determine which antecedents are invariably attendant to which consequents and thus identify causal links.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use controlled separation/variation of antecedent facts in experiments to isolate causal contributions. Mental analysis suggests which separations to attempt; experiment performs them in nature to reveal actual dependencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualities of a Good Observer
rubrics_metrics.description: Good observation involves seeing the component parts of phenomena, attending in the right places, distinguishing observation from imagination or inference, and recording both kinds and degrees (not only whether but how much).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid inattention, over-inference, vagueness in quantities, and awkward partitioning (merging things that should be separated or vice versa). Train to note degree as well as kind, and to separate what is seen from what is inferred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules for Observing are Rules of Self-education, Not an Art of Doing
rubrics_metrics.description: There is not a mechanical 'Art of Observing' that teaches how to perform observation; rather, rules for observing are instructions to prepare and cultivate the mind so that it is fit to observe or invent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement observation training as intellectual and educative preparation (habits of attention, methods of decomposition), rather than expecting simple procedural checklists to suffice. Cultivate mental qualities that make precise observation possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Algebraic Extension to Represent Opposing Effects
rubrics_metrics.description: When concurrent causes produce opposite effects, conceive of the joint effect as the sum that may include negative quantities (addition of opposites), enabling algebraic treatment of differences as well as sums.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply algebraic ideas (negative quantities) conceptually to model opposing causal effects (e.g., inflow vs outflow). This conceptual tool legitimizes representing 'difference' as a form of addition and extends quantitative reasoning.
